Development transparency and review status

ICORE was developed in an iterative human–GPT workflow. Substantial portions of its implementation and documentation were generated and revised with GPT, under human direction.

Not all implementation details or documentation claims have undergone independent human review. The reported automated tests and benchmarks cover only the tested cases and environments; they do not establish correctness for all inputs or replace an independent code review.

Treat this release as research software. Review and validate it for your application before relying on it, particularly in safety-critical systems.

This note concerns ICORE-owned code and documentation, not third-party dependencies, which retain their original authorship and licenses.

How to read. Start with Section 1, even if your goal is the C/C++ code. Open the expandable excerpts only when a concept is clear. Every teal source link opens the exact embedded file, with line numbers and the relevant function highlighted. The second section names each optimization, its benefit, and the condition that makes it valid.

Evidence matters. The animated teaching examples are independently computed, small reference problems—not invented production telemetry. Actual instrumented ICORE replays appear separately in Section 2.16. The namespace migration preserves tested arithmetic; version 0.20.0 denotes the public API/ABI rename, not a new numerical algorithm.

Scope: native C11/C++17 implementation and the retained 393-example interface. The optional JAX engine is identified separately. Linux/x86-64 checks are reported; Apple Silicon performance and exhaustive numerical correctness are not claimed.

Section 1

1. The algorithm

From a constrained decision to a checked Newton step: derive the equations, watch the iterations, and connect each mathematical object to the current implementation.

1.1

What are we asking the computer to decide?

A trajectory is a sequence of decisions. The solver chooses the entire sequence together, subject to equations and limits.

Imagine choosing a vehicle's acceleration over a finite horizon. A state describes what the system is doing now: position and velocity, for example. A control describes what we choose: acceleration, steering, or thrust. Choosing a control at time 0 changes the state at time 1, which changes what will be possible at time 2. Optimizing each control independently would ignore this connection.

Let be the state, the control, and the stage vector. The order control first, state second matters: it is also the native array convention. There are N transitions and N+1 state stages. There is no physical terminal control; native storage has terminal control slots whose cost and constraint coefficients must be zero.

Here H is a positive-semidefinite quadratic cost matrix. A quadratic cost can represent tracking error, effort, and cross terms. The linear term can shift the target without changing curvature. The dynamics are affine, not nonlinear: the b term supplies an offset. A nonlinear trajectory optimizer can repeatedly form problems of this kind, but that outer nonlinear algorithm is not this solver.

The cone is a product of scalar nonnegative coordinates and Lorentz/second-order-cone blocks. A scalar coordinate says “this slack is nonnegative.” An SOC block says “its leading coordinate is at least the Euclidean norm of its remaining coordinates.” This covers ordinary bounds and norm limits in a unified notation. It does not imply support for every convex cone: exponential, power, and general semidefinite matrix cones are not implemented by the current native model.

For ordinary inequalities, the equation Gv+s=h means exactly Gv≤h. The slack is the available room before a limit. For , use G=1, h=3, and s=3−u. For , use two rows, u≤3 and −u≤3. A slack is not an extra physical degree of freedom; the constraint equation determines it once v is known.

Convexity matters. With a convex quadratic objective and affine/conic constraints, a feasible point satisfying the KKT conditions described below is globally optimal under the appropriate duality conditions. Numerical termination checks approximate these conditions. They are not a proof that an arbitrarily nonconvex input is safe, and they do not turn a numerical failure into a certificate of infeasibility.

Two input representations, three native computational bodies

An OCP dictionary can remain a general stage model, qualify for the small dense-QP specialization, or pass an exact structural reduction to the affine physical-chain representation. A directly supplied ChainQP uses the latter representation. These choices change algebra and storage, not the definition of the requested objective or stopping tolerance.

1.2

From an objective to an optimality system

Gradients tell us how cost changes. Multipliers explain why a constrained optimum can have a nonzero cost gradient.

For the next derivation, collect all unfixed decision variables into a single vector v. This is mathematical notation, not a prescription to build a huge dense matrix in production. Let Ev=b represent all affine equalities and let Gv+s=h represent the cone constraints. Reusing the letter b here denotes the assembled equality right-hand side; stage offsets in the native dynamics have the sign shown in the previous chapter.

The gradient is Hv+c. In an unconstrained quadratic problem, setting this gradient to zero gives the optimum when H is positive definite. Constraints change the story. At a lower bound v≥0, moving toward a negative unconstrained minimizer is forbidden. The objective gradient need not vanish because an opposing constraint force can balance it.

Introduce an unrestricted equality multiplier y and a cone multiplier z in the dual cone. The cones implemented here are self-dual, so z belongs to the same cone as s. Consider the Lagrangian, with the slack eliminated only for writing the constraint contribution:

The stationarity equation is . Think of y and z as prices for violating the equations and limits. For a scalar inequality, z≥0: tightening an active upper limit cannot have a negative local price under this sign convention. Complementarity says the unused room and the price cannot both remain positive at an exact optimum. A nonbinding limit has room and zero price; a binding limit can have a positive price and zero room.

For scalar inequalities, the symbol ∘ means elementwise multiplication. For SOC blocks it means the Jordan product, derived in Chapter 1.8. These are nonlinear equations only because complementarity multiplies two unknowns. That is the nonlinearity the interior-point iteration must solve even when the original optimization problem is convex and quadratic.

A beginner-friendly way to test the signs is the one-variable problem subject to v≤1. At the solution v=1 and s=0. Stationarity is v−2+z=0, so z=1. Changing the inequality to −v≤−1 requires changing the G sign, not merely changing the name of the multiplier.

The KKT system also explains why a solver returns more than a trajectory. Primal variables answer “what do we do?” Multipliers, slacks, and residuals answer “how do we know it is a solution?” If a presolve eliminated variables, the library must reconstruct these quantities in the original coordinates before claiming success.

Symbol dictionary

v: decision vector. x/u: state/control. s: primal cone slack. z: cone multiplier. y: equality multiplier. H/c: quadratic and linear cost. E/b: equality data. G/h: conic inequality data. λ: the scaled cone vector, not a physical state or an equality multiplier.

Code convention to keep straight

The OCP implementation uses nu_t for terminal equality multipliers, whereas nu is also the control dimension in workspace definitions. In this book, the terminal multiplier is written ν and the control dimension is written nᵤ. A native lambda buffer can hold direct orthant ratios when that representation tag is active; do not infer its meaning from the pointer name alone.

1.3

Why stay inside a cone?

The boundary contains the answer, but the interior gives us invertible local equations on the way there.

At an exact scalar optimum, some products sᵢzᵢ vanish. Trying to impose zero products immediately can make it unclear which side of each pair should be zero. An interior-point method instead keeps both s and z strictly inside their cones and asks their products to become small together.

For positive scalar slacks, the logarithmic barrier grows without bound when any sᵢ approaches zero. Minimizing the objective plus this barrier while satisfying the equalities leads to a perturbed complementarity equation. A sequence of smaller positive μ values traces a central path under suitable regularity assumptions.

For μ large, the algorithm tolerates a nonzero complementarity product. As μ decreases, it can approach active boundaries. This does not mean ICORE repeatedly solves an unrelated unconstrained barrier problem to completion for a fixed schedule of μ. It is a primal-dual predictor-corrector method: each iteration estimates how far an aggressive affine step could go, then computes a centering target from that estimate.

There is another crucial distinction: interior is not the same as primal feasible. The implementation is allowed to start with positive s and z even if Gv+s−h or Ev−b is nonzero. Newton's equations reduce those residuals. Until they are sufficiently small, v can violate the original inequality Gv≤h even while the stored s is positive. The teaching path below intentionally demonstrates this. Do not draw every iterate inside the feasible polygon merely because the method is called an interior-point method.

The product-cone complementarity measure in this implementation is a sum over the retained blocks: absolute scalar products for orthant entries and the absolute Euclidean sᵀz pairing for each SOC. When cone membership holds, these pairings are nonnegative in exact arithmetic. The absolute-value and stable evaluation rules help detect or avoid numerical cancellation; they are not substitutes for membership checks.

This d is the code's normalization. It counts one SOC block once, regardless of its vector length. Some references use a different barrier/trace normalization and describe rank-two SOC contributions. Importing that normalization without changing the other formulas would be an implementation mistake. In this book the conventions are chosen to match the actual degree passed to the shared driver.

Constant constraints require special care. A row that contains no effective variable does not need a barrier iteration. But it still has an original feasibility condition. The implementation removes eligible constant orthant rows or constant SOC blocks from the iterative cone work and retains their original feasibility defect in the stopping test. Dropping them without that defect check would allow an infeasible constant model to be accepted.

What μ is not

μ is not the user tolerance, and it is not the objective value. The final test checks primal residual, dual residual, and the total gap, each against the requested absolute tolerance. A small average gap μ alone is insufficient when many constraints are present.

1.4

Three residuals that make success meaningful

Every fast path must ultimately answer the original equations, not just an easier internally scaled system.

Define the three equation residual vectors at the current iterate:

The stationarity residual r_d is a vector, not an objective difference. The infinity norm of a vector is its largest absolute component. In the native OCP body, the primal scalar test combines dynamics residuals, terminal equalities, slack equations, constant-model defects, and negative cone margins. The dual scalar test combines stationarity and negative dual-cone margins. The gap is the aggregate complementarity pairing. All must be finite.

The equality terms must be interpreted in the original model's units. A constraint measured in meters and a stationarity equation associated with a very large cost coefficient can have very different natural magnitudes. This implementation uses absolute outer thresholds; it does not silently choose a weaker tolerance for a difficult named test problem. Consequently, model scaling affects numerical conditioning and the interpretation of a requested tolerance.

For an SOC vector a=(a₀,aₜ), the cone margin is . A positive margin means strict interior, zero means boundary, and a negative margin means violation. Checking only a₀>0 is wrong: (1,2,0) has a positive head but lies outside the cone. For an orthant vector, the margin is the smallest component.

Why check original residuals after presolve? Suppose an exact structural reduction eliminated fixed coordinates or an epigraph representation. Floating-point recovery can still be wrong because of an indexing, scaling, or sign error. The Python layer recovers the original coordinates and checks their equations. A successfully solved reduced model is downgraded if its recovered original-model residual does not satisfy the required test.

Why not stop on objective change? Two inaccurate iterates may have nearly identical objective values. Conversely, an objective can change by tiny relative amounts while a physically important equality is still violated. The implementation's termination criterion is an approximate optimality certificate, not a stagnation heuristic.

Native and Python defaults differ

The Python Solver default tolerance is 1e−8. The low-level native default-options function uses 1e−7. The catalog runner explicitly requests 1e−8. Both interfaces use an iteration cap of 200 and five refinement steps by default. Always record the effective options rather than assuming that a default in one interface applies to another.

1.5

Derive the Newton system instead of memorizing it

The expensive step is a linear solve. Its exact signs and eliminated variables determine whether the solver is correct.

First take the orthant-only case. At the current iterate, S=diag(s) and Z=diag(z). A Newton direction is a proposed change (Δv,Δy,Δs,Δz). Linearize each KKT equation. The first three equations are already affine, so their linearization is exact. Complementarity supplies a diagonal coupling.

Let b_c denote the desired right-hand side of the linearized product equation. We will set it differently for the predictor and corrector. The system is:

A direct implementation could solve for all four blocks simultaneously. That wastes the fact that S and Z are diagonal. Eliminate Δs using the slack equation, then substitute it into the product equation:

Substitution into stationarity leaves a smaller equality-constrained system:

The matrix M is the cost curvature plus positive constraint curvature. Near an active constraint, z/s can become very large. The optimization problem can be well posed while this particular eliminated system becomes poorly conditioned. This is one reason the implementation contains scaling, alternative factorizations, and refinement rather than a single unconditional Cholesky call.

Notice what is fixed between predictor and corrector at the same iterate: H, G, E, s, z, Γ, and therefore M. Only b_c changes. This makes it possible to factor once and solve more than one right-hand side. After an accepted iterate update, s and z have changed; the Newton factors generally must change too. Reusing them across arbitrary iterations would be a different algorithm, not the harmless reuse described here.

In a stage OCP, E couples adjacent stages and G is stage local. Therefore M remains block diagonal by stage, while the saddle system has a chain structure. Riccati recursion solves precisely this smaller structured problem. In a certified dense specialization, the equalities and fixed state can be eliminated first. In the affine-chain representation, the slack and epigraph elimination produces a block-tridiagonal physical-variable system. The shared outer algorithm can therefore call different linear algebra without changing these KKT goals.

A useful debugging test is to take any computed direction, reconstruct Δs and Δz, and evaluate all four original linearized equations. Testing only MΔv≈rhs can miss a sign error in slack recovery or a stale equality right-hand side. The production refinement machinery evaluates block residuals for this reason.

chain_form_rhs · source excerpt
 112  static int chain_form_rhs(void *context, double target, int corrector)
 113  {
 114      chain_context *c = (chain_context *)context;
 115      chain_workspace *w = c->w;
 116      int i, m = w->m;
 117      const double *s = w->state + w->nv + w->nd, *z = s + m;
 118      const double *ads = w->affine + w->nv + w->nd, *adz = ads + m;
 119      double *bc = w->target + w->nv + w->nd + m;
 120      if (corrector)
 121          for (i = 0; i < m; ++i)
 122              bc[i] = -s[i] * z[i] - ads[i] * adz[i] + target;
 123      else
 124          for (i = 0; i < m; ++i)
 125              bc[i] = -s[i] * z[i];
 126      return 1;
 127  }
1.6

Predictor, centering, and the second-order correction

An aggressive trial estimates progress; a second solve corrects the curvature of complementarity.

The affine predictor asks for complementarity to become zero in the linearized equations, with no centering target. In the notation of the previous chapter:

Solve once, producing an affine direction. Then find the maximum admissible primal and dual steps separately, each clipped to one. For the orthant, only negative direction components restrict a positive vector:

Use those two steps to predict the average complementarity after the affine move. This is a prediction for choosing centering, not necessarily the step that will be applied to the iterate.

If the affine prediction removes most complementarity, σ is small: use little centering. If it predicts little improvement, σ is closer to one: aim for a more central iterate. The cube is the implemented predictor-corrector heuristic, not a theorem that all problems need this exponent. The method is in the Mehrotra predictor-corrector family; the derivation here follows the implemented residual equations rather than reproducing a paper's notation.

[1]

Why does the corrector contain a product of affine directions? Expand the product at a full step:

The Newton linearization omits the last, quadratic term. The affine direction gives an inexpensive estimate of it. The corrector right-hand side cancels this estimate and adds the centering target:

ICORE solves for the combined corrected direction using this right-hand side and the same stationarity/equality/slack residuals. Do not compute this combined direction and then add the affine direction again. That double counts the predictor. Some presentations instead define a separate correction increment; their equations must be interpreted consistently before translating them into code.

The factors are ordinarily reused for the corrector. A numerical recovery can legitimately refactor at the same iterate: for example, an unacceptable mixed-precision direction can force a double-precision retry. “Factor once” describes the ordinary predictor-corrector path, not a promise that recovery never occurs.

There is also a narrowly guarded early finish for certain orthant QPs. If the affine step is almost full and predicts an already-small gap, the callback can test the actual trial point against tightened original residual requirements and accept it without a corrector solve. The prediction alone cannot declare success. This is a final-step certificate, not an active-set solver or a change in tolerance.

Bookkeeping rule

Keep the affine Δs and Δz alive until the corrector right-hand side has been formed and all recovery paths that may rebuild it have finished. A scratch-buffer reuse that overwrites them can preserve the predictor solution yet corrupt the corrector. This lifetime is one of the key invariants documented in Section 2.

1.7

Watch a complete interior-point solve

This small, independently computed example exposes every predictor and corrector quantity.

We solve a two-variable quadratic with nonnegative coordinates and a sum constraint. The unconstrained target lies outside the feasible triangle, so at least one limit must be active at the solution.

The initial v=(0.15,0.15), s=(1,1,1), and z=(1,1,1) are interior in the slack/dual variables but do not satisfy the slack equation. The first corrected primal iterate slightly exceeds the sum constraint. That is not a plotting error: this is an infeasible-start primal-dual iteration. The equations drive the mismatch to zero while s and z remain positive.

The plotted path and table come from tutorials/minimal_ipm.py, which implements the derivation above using NumPy's dense Cholesky and triangular solves. It does not claim to execute every production fast path. Its final solution is checked separately against the native implementation. Drag the iteration slider, press Play, or step manually. The affine arrow is a prediction; the corrected arrow is the direction actually damped and applied by the teaching solver.

Read the output in this order. First inspect r_p and r_d: these measure feasibility and stationarity rather than centering. Next inspect gap and μ. Then compare μ_aff with μ and observe the resulting σ. Finally inspect α: a nearly full step can be safe late in the solve, while a limited admissible direction requires damping.

At the last iterate the sum constraint has almost zero slack and a positive dual multiplier. The lower bounds retain positive slack and tiny multipliers. Complementarity is therefore satisfied by different members of different pairs becoming small. This is exactly the mechanism that avoids guessing the active set before the solve.

The displayed Newton defects test the original linearized equations. They are small in this well-scaled example. In a real OCP they may require refinement or a safer factorization. Section 2 explains why simply printing the objective or a successful Cholesky return code would be inadequate validation.

  19  def solve_qp(H: np.ndarray, c: np.ndarray, G: np.ndarray, h: np.ndarray,
  20               *, tolerance: float = 1e-10, max_iterations: int = 60) -> dict:
  21      H, c, G, h = map(lambda a: np.asarray(a, dtype=np.float64), (H, c, G, h))
  22      n, m = len(c), len(h)
  23      if H.shape != (n,n) or G.shape != (m,n) or m == 0:
  24          raise ValueError('This teaching example requires a finite, orthant-only QP.')
  25      if not all(np.isfinite(a).all() for a in (H,c,G,h)):
  26          raise ValueError('Nonfinite coefficient.')
  27      v = np.full(n, .15)
  28      s, z = np.ones(m), np.ones(m)
  29      records = []
  30      for iteration in range(max_iterations + 1):
  31          rd = H @ v + c + G.T @ z
  32          rp = G @ v + s - h
  33          gap = float(s @ z)
  34          primal, dual = float(np.linalg.norm(rp, np.inf)), float(np.linalg.norm(rd, np.inf))
  35          record = dict(iteration=iteration, v=v.tolist(), s=s.tolist(), z=z.tolist(),
  36                        rd=rd.tolist(), rp=rp.tolist(), primal=primal, dual=dual,
  37                        gap=gap, mu=gap/m, objective=float(.5*v@H@v+c@v))
  38          records.append(record)
  39          if max(primal,dual,gap) <= tolerance:
  40              return dict(status='solved', records=records, v=v.tolist(), objective=record['objective'])
  41          if iteration == max_iterations:
  42              break
  43          gamma = z/s
  44          M = H + G.T @ (gamma[:,None]*G)
  45          L = np.linalg.cholesky(M)
  46  
  47          def direction(bc):
  48              rhs = -rd - G.T @ (bc/s + gamma*rp)
  49              dv = np.linalg.solve(L.T, np.linalg.solve(L, rhs))
  50              ds = -rp - G @ dv
  51              dz = (bc-z*ds)/s
  52              defect = max(np.linalg.norm(H@dv+G.T@dz+rd,np.inf),
  53                           np.linalg.norm(G@dv+ds+rp,np.inf),
  54                           np.linalg.norm(z*ds+s*dz-bc,np.inf))
  55              return dv, ds, dz, float(defect)

  59          mu_aff = max(0.,float((s+ap*ds_a)@(z+ad*dz_a)))/m
  60          sigma = min(1.,max(0.,mu_aff/(gap/m)))**3
  61          bc = sigma*(gap/m)*np.ones(m)-s*z-ds_a*dz_a
  62          dv,ds,dz,corrector_error = direction(bc)
  63          admissible = min(boundary_step(s,ds),boundary_step(z,dz))
  64          alpha = admissible*((1-admissible)*.99+admissible*.9999999)
  65          for backtracks in range(20):
  66              if np.all(s+alpha*ds>0) and np.all(z+alpha*dz>0):
  67                  break
  68              alpha *= .5
  69          else:
  70              raise FloatingPointError('No interior step in the teaching example.')

  72                        dv=dv.tolist(),ds=ds.tolist(),dz=dz.tolist(),gamma=gamma.tolist(),

1.8

A second-order cone is one coupled constraint block

Its coordinates are not independent nonnegative numbers. Its geometry determines scaling and admissible steps.

A Lorentz cone of dimension p is

For a thrust limit , the cone slack can be (T,u) after the appropriate affine sign convention. Replacing this with componentwise bounds would define a box, not the same norm ball. The coupled geometry must survive both the model adapter and the Newton algebra.

A useful scalar analogue of multiplication is the SOC Jordan product:

The identity e acts like the number one. The product's head is the Euclidean pairing aᵀb. Thus a central complementarity relation has sᵀz=μ per SOC block under this convention. This is why the implemented degree normalization counts an SOC once.

The eigenvalue-like coordinates of an SOC vector are and . Both are positive in the interior. Their product is the Lorentz determinant . Near the boundary the small coordinate tends to zero. Directly subtracting two large squares to obtain this determinant can be inaccurate even though the positive head-minus-radius difference can still be represented.

The linear map has a special arrow structure. There is no need to allocate and factor a dense p×p matrix to solve Lₐq=b. Eliminating the tail yields:

The denominator can be written , avoiding a direct difference of squares. The production corrector also uses extended-precision accumulation for selected cancellation-sensitive scalar quantities. That does not make the whole solver a long-double implementation; the outer arrays remain double precision.

A maximum SOC step requires both a nonnegative head and a nonnegative Lorentz determinant along a+αΔa. The latter is a quadratic in α. A stable implementation must handle quadratic, nearly linear, and nonrestricting cases, choose the relevant positive boundary, and guard against roundoff. The final strict-interior test remains essential even after a computed boundary step. ICORE uses norm and range-aware cone routines rather than treating every component as a scalar bound.

A stable pairing identity

For interior SOC vectors, the radial/angular expression below equals the ordinary Euclidean dot product. Near complementary opposite tails, it avoids subtracting two nearly equal large terms.

If either tail norm is zero, the implementation uses the corresponding simpler head product. The normalized-tail expression is never evaluated with a zero radius.

soc_pair · source excerpt
   1  /* Cone arithmetic, residual statistics, scaling, and admissible steps.
   2   * Scalar inequalities use positive slacks; SOC blocks use radial and angular parts.
   3   * Direct orthant scaling and general cone scaling solve the same Newton equations.
   4   * Private implementation: included exactly once by ocp.c. */
   5  
   6  /* The radial/angular expression stays nonnegative even at complementarity. */
   7  static double soc_pair(const double *a, const double *b, int n)
   8  {
   9      double ra = norm2(a + 1, n - 1), rb = norm2(b + 1, n - 1), angular = 0.0;
  10      int i;
  11      if (ra == 0.0 || rb == 0.0)
  12          return a[0] * b[0];
  13      for (i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
  14          double u = a[i] / ra + b[i] / rb;
  15          angular += u * u;
  16      }
  17      return (a[0] - ra) * b[0] + ra * (b[0] - rb) + 0.5 * ra * rb * angular;
  18  }
1.9

Nesterov–Todd scaling: balance the primal and dual cones

One symmetric coordinate change makes the two sides of complementarity meet at a shared scaled point.

For an orthant, dividing by s is straightforward. For an SOC, the direct Jordan-product Jacobian is not the convenient symmetric system we want to factor. Nesterov–Todd scaling supplies a symmetric positive-definite cone-preserving operator W satisfying

This is the convention used here and in the native cone code. Other software can use the reciprocal operator or a transpose convention; copying formulas without checking that convention causes subtle errors. For scalar coordinates, and .

The following construction explains the SOC implementation. Normalize s and z by square roots of their Lorentz determinants, denoted d_s and d_z. In exact arithmetic:

Set ρ=‖a‖, n=a/ρ when ρ>0, t=√(1+ρ²), and η=√d_s/√d_z. When ρ=0, take the spatial block as identity and the off-diagonal block as zero. Then

The matrix is a positive scale times a Lorentz boost. It stretches one head/axis direction and compresses the other by reciprocal amounts. Forming it as a dense matrix is useful in a teaching test but unnecessary in production. The implementation stores the unit axis n, η, and the large boost eigenvalue β=t+ρ. The small eigenvalue is evaluated as 1/β, not as t−ρ. That reciprocal avoids catastrophic cancellation when t≈ρ is large.

For a vector a, split its tail into a component parallel to n and an orthogonal component. Only the head and parallel component need the two eigenvalue combinations; the orthogonal tail is unchanged by the unit boost. The native boost_apply therefore applies W or W⁻¹ with dot products and vector operations, not a p×p matrix multiplication.

After applying the two routes, the code forms . In exact arithmetic they are identical; averaging reduces asymmetry from finite precision. Both the determinant and the resulting λ must pass interior/finite checks. If a range or positivity check fails, it is a numerical failure or a trigger for an existing alternative path, not permission to continue with an invalid scaling.

[2][3]

In scaled coordinates, define and . The symmetric predictor/corrector relation is

For orthant blocks this reduces to the scalar formula derived earlier. For SOC blocks it is the NT-symmetrized direction, not an instruction to use an arbitrary unsymmetrized Jordan Jacobian. The factorization-friendly system becomes

Eliminating the cone block gives with , and right-hand side . Once Δv and Δz are known, either slack equation or scaled complementarity recovers Δs; a residual check verifies their consistency.

These equations explain the implementation's arrays: the factor kernels need scaled constraint rows; the cone routines need the compact scaling operator; the corrector needs preserved affine directions; and the refinement test needs the original unregularized equations. It would be incorrect to assume that all of these buffers describe the same coordinates merely because their lengths match.

boost_apply · source excerpt
 233  /* SOC boost: b[0] is its large eigenvalue, b[1:] its unit axis.
 234   * Its other eigenvalue is computed as 1/b[0], not by subtraction.
 235   * Thus no rounded identity w0*w0-|wt|^2==1 is assumed. */
 236  ICORE_OCP_INLINE void boost_apply(const double *b, double eta, const double *v, double *out, int n,
 237                               int inverse)
 238  {
 239      double p = dot(b + 1, v + 1, n - 1), large = b[0], small = 1.0 / large;
 240      double plus, minus, head, parallel, fac = inverse ? 1.0 / eta : eta;
 241      int i;
 242      if (inverse) {
 243          double t = large;
 244          large = small;
 245          small = t;
 246      }
 247      plus = large * (v[0] + p);
 248      minus = small * (v[0] - p);
 249      head = 0.5 * (plus + minus);
 250      parallel = 0.5 * (plus - minus);
 251      out[0] = fac * head;
 252      for (i = 1; i < n; ++i)
 253          out[i] = fac * (v[i] + b[i] * (parallel - p));
 254  }
1.10

Riccati recursion is structured block elimination

The backward pass eliminates a control block; the forward pass reconstructs the trajectory. No matrix inverse is formed.

After cone elimination, one Newton direction is an equality-constrained quadratic subproblem with stage Hessians . The equality right-hand sides are residual corrections, not necessarily the physical model offsets. To derive the linear algebra without sign clutter, write a generic affine dynamics subproblem

where ξ and υ can denote Newton state/control increments. Let its stage cost be

The Q/R/S in this chapter are the current Newton subproblem blocks, including constraint curvature. They need not equal the original unaugmented cost blocks. Suppose all future stages have already been eliminated, leaving a quadratic value function . Substitute the dynamics into this value function and collect terms:

Stationarity with respect to the local control is . Factor , and solve triangular systems to obtain feedback and feedforward terms:

The inverse symbols describe a mathematical solution; production code does not construct those inverses. Substitute the minimizing control back into the quadratic to obtain

Start with the terminal cost and work backward from N−1 to 0. Then, starting from the fixed initial state/increment, reconstruct controls and states forward. Equality multipliers can be recovered from the value-function derivatives using the dynamics sign convention. The implementation's packed L/T/P and affine sweep arrays store equivalent triangular-solve quantities, not necessarily explicit K and k arrays.

This is also block Gaussian elimination of the KKT matrix. Dynamic-programming language and sparse-linear-algebra language describe the same calculation here. The advantage is that each stage touches only local blocks and the next stage's message. For fixed state and control dimensions, work and storage scale linearly with horizon length. This says nothing about linear scaling when state dimension itself grows: dense local block operations are cubic in relevant dimensions and their memory traffic matters.

The lab contains nonzero affine offsets, cross costs, and linear terms. These are important tests: an implementation that only works for zero right-hand sides can produce attractive factor timings while failing the actual Newton solve. A dense KKT comparison is a convenient independent oracle for small examples, not the recommended production method for a long horizon.

One subtle boundary optimization follows from the derivation. In a Newton solve with fixed initial state, Δx₀=0. Terms that only multiply this zero vector need not be computed. But the auxiliary initializer may solve with the nonzero physical initial state. It must not reuse an incomplete stage-zero factor intended only for a zero Newton boundary. The code carries explicit validity checks for this distinction.

1.11

Terminal constraints and epigraph variables

Borders and eliminable local variables can preserve the chain structure, but only with exact certificates.

A terminal equation F x_N=f couples the final state to an additional multiplier ν. One approach would append it to a large dense KKT system. The structured approach instead solves the dynamics-constrained system with a small border.

Let T represent the inverse action of the already structured, dynamics-constrained Hessian on allowable primal directions. This is conceptual notation: T is applied through Riccati sweeps, not explicitly formed. Let C select the terminal equation in the full primal coordinates. With an unconstrained-border solution d₀, the full direction has the form

Here the desired terminal correction is Cd=−r_F. The small matrix CTCᵀ is a terminal Schur complement. The implementation accumulates its contributions along the backward recursion, solves the small terminal system, and includes its effect during recovery. It normalizes terminal rows for algebra and recovers multipliers in the original row units. Normalized multipliers cannot be returned as if they belonged to the original F.

Partial factorization recovery makes this bookkeeping delicate. If a failed stage already contributed to the terminal Schur sum, retrying that suffix without restoring a checkpoint can double count it. The suffix repair code saves or rebuilds the relevant terminal contribution together with the factors. A “local” factor repair that ignores this border is not correct.

Now consider an absolute-value penalty , with w≥0. Introduce an epigraph variable t and the pair

The epigraph t has no quadratic cost and participates only in this pair. Its Newton curvature can be eliminated locally. Write and . The weighted pair contributes the following Hessian on the physical residual and t:

Eliminating the t block leaves physical curvature

The final expression is the stable evaluation used in the chain body. Directly subtracting the nearly equal first two terms is particularly bad when one weight dominates. Eliminating t also changes the right-hand side; retaining only the curvature formula would produce a wrong Newton direction. The code stores reciprocal and ratio terms for that recovery.

The OCP epigraph recognizer is intentionally restrictive. A leading t control must be absent from the cost Hessian and dynamics, appear in exactly two orthant rows with coefficient −1 and zero right-hand sides, and have a valid distinct partner with coefficients ±1. A partner appearing in another inequality invalidates this simple certificate. The recognizer uses exact coefficients, not a problem name or a loose numerical “looks like” test.

1.12

Cholesky, square roots, QR, and regularization

They solve related algebra, but they expose different numerical weaknesses. “Square root” does not always mean “QR everywhere.”

For a symmetric positive-definite matrix M, Cholesky computes a lower triangular L with M=LLᵀ. It is efficient because it uses symmetry and does not need pivoting in exact arithmetic. Riccati recursion applies Cholesky to local control or state blocks and builds Schur complements. When the mathematical matrix is semidefinite, poorly scaled, or damaged by roundoff, a tiny or negative computed pivot needs careful treatment.

A small nonnegative regularization shifts the factorization system. The Python default is 1e−11. The implementation uses this regularization in its local factors, along with existing pivot floors and checks. It must still evaluate residuals of the original unregularized Newton equations and the original model. Otherwise, solving a nearby easier problem could be mislabeled as solving the requested one.

Equilibration rescales a matrix to reduce large differences in row/column magnitudes. If D is a positive diagonal scaling, a solve with DMD and appropriately scaled vectors is mathematically equivalent before rounding. The equilibrated recovery is rebuilt from the original block, not from a partially overwritten failed Cholesky factor. If the recovery fails, the original fallback sequence remains available.

Why preserve original square roots? Suppose M=TᵀT. Forming M explicitly squares the condition number of T and can lose a small positive direction when subtracting large terms. QR factorization T=QR gives M=RᵀR without first constructing all cancellation-prone normal-equation entries. The same idea can be applied to a stage stack containing original cost roots, scaled constraint rows, regularization rows, and the propagated next-stage root.

The partition and elimination of control/state columns then extract the desired stage factor. The production implementation distinguishes packed square-root Riccati operations, local QR repair, suffix QR repair, and a whole-chain QR path. A packed square-root route can use Cholesky-like packed operations and local recovery; it is not synonymous with redoing every stage through Householder QR on every iteration.

The automatic mode first attempts eligible efficient packed work. If a required diagonal-only preparation cannot be used, it rebuilds the full stage Hessian before classical recovery. Classical factorization can repair a suffix from original roots. If the chain remains unacceptable, a full square-root/QR recovery is attempted. Forced classical and forced square-root modes are real policy overrides; they do not have the same fallback menu as AUTO.

The QR suffix is not constructed from an already cancellation-damaged P and declared “stable.” It rebuilds the required range from original coefficient roots, and the boundary moves monotonically so a successful stage is not repeatedly refactored in one repair attempt. Exact-symmetry and minimum-regularization guards also apply to that shortcut. These details explain why the code has more branches than a textbook Riccati recursion.

1.13

Iterative refinement and mixed precision

A factor can be approximate if the residual is checked accurately and corrections actually improve it.

Even a successful factorization gives an approximate direction. Let Kd=b denote the original Newton system, and let the available factor solve an approximation . Compute r=b−Kd using the original coefficients, solve , and propose d←d+δ. This is iterative refinement.

In ICORE, a correction is accepted only if the checked block residual improves. Trial directions and trial residuals are stored separately so a rejected correction does not destroy the best accepted direction. Five refinement slots are the default; a special recovery proposal can consume a slot from that existing budget rather than creating hidden unlimited work.

The default inner target is , unless the user supplies a strictly positive explicit refinement tolerance. This inner test uses normalized block residuals relative to the corresponding Newton right-hand sides. It is not the same numerical quantity as the absolute outer feasibility/stationarity/gap test.

A crucial implementation nuance: the ordinary double-precision direction routines can finish after bounded refinement with a finite direction even when their desired inner target was not reached. They do not all make “inner target reached” an unconditional acceptance requirement. The outer solver still must satisfy the original final KKT test. The mixed-precision path is stricter: an unacceptable mixed direction must trigger its double-precision retry. Claiming that every accepted Newton direction in every body always meets the inner tolerance would misdescribe this source.

Mixed precision uses FP32 for selected factor/sweep operations while retaining FP64 outer state and residuals. It is not enabled on every model. The automatic candidate requires the eligible diagonal-cost, orthant-only packed OCP structure, no epigraph or terminal border, and a zero initial Newton direction. Explicit inner tolerance disables the adaptive mixed policy. The current auto forcing rule is

Far from the solution, the linear system need not be solved to final outer accuracy if its direction is adequate. Near convergence, the implementation returns to full double precision. These constants are policy choices in this revision, not universally optimal numerical thresholds.

When a mixed direction fails its residual/finite checks, the code disables the mixed route, invalidates its sweep tokens, reconstructs the canonical right-hand side, factors in FP64 at the same iterate, and retries. For the corrector, the preserved affine slack/dual directions must still be available. Reusing a refinement residual buffer as if it were the original right-hand side would solve a different equation.

1.14

How much of the direction is taken?

Boundary geometry limits the step; an explicit interior check is the final guard.

A Newton direction is not automatically safe at full length. A negative slack direction can cross zero; an SOC direction can cross the curved cone boundary. The callbacks compute separate primal and dual admissible steps. The shared driver uses their minimum, clipped to the callback's [0,1] range, as the corrected admissible step a.

Under the fixed policy, the step is θa with default θ=0.99. Under the adaptive policy, it is

This retains conservative damping for a small admissible step and approaches a full step when a is close to one. AUTO selects this adaptive policy for an orthant-only problem, but uses fixed damping when curved cones are present. An explicit ADAPTIVE choice has its own semantics; AUTO must not be described as making the same choice for SOCs.

The algorithm then tests that the actual trial slacks and duals are strictly interior. If not, it halves α, at most twenty attempts. This backtracking is not an objective-merit-function or filter line search. It is a numerical cone-interiority guard. There is no claim that the objective decreases on every infeasible-start primal-dual iteration.

The same α updates all primal and dual iterate blocks in the ordinary corrected step. The separate affine primal and dual steps were used to estimate μ_aff, not to maintain two independently advanced production iterates. If there are no retained cone constraints, there is no complementarity corrector; the equality-constrained direction is taken with the appropriate full-step logic and finite checks.

Failure to find a positive finite interior step is a numerical failure. Reaching the iteration cap is an iteration-limit status. An invalid model and allocation failure have separate statuses. None of these is a general infeasibility certificate. The current core does not implement a homogeneous self-dual embedding that certifies arbitrary infeasible or unbounded conic models.

1.15

Cold starts, cached initializers, and model updates

Reusing an auxiliary factor is not the same as warm-starting from yesterday’s solution.

An interior-point solver needs positive slack and dual cone variables before it can divide or form NT scaling. It also benefits from an initial primal/equality guess related to the model. The native OCP initializer can solve an auxiliary equality-constrained system, evaluate residual slacks, and shift the cone variables into their interiors. A certified single-variable-bound case has a simpler initializer.

The auxiliary system uses identity cone scaling rather than the current Newton scaling of a solved iterate. For eligible orthant models, initialization can normalize rows whose coefficients are large: use a divisor based on max(1,max|g|), and transform the initial slack/dual variables consistently back to original units. Small rows are not amplified. This scaling is for the auxiliary initializer, not a replacement for original-model residual evaluation. If the normalized initialization fails, the existing unnormalized initializer remains a checked retry.

There are several distinct caches. A completed cold initial point can be reused only when all inputs affecting it are still valid. An auxiliary factor may remain valid across some right-hand-side changes even when the initial point must be recomputed. Immutable packed cost/dynamics/constraint data can survive coefficient-preserving updates. Current Newton factors depend on the current scaling; predictor/corrector products and direction tokens have much shorter lifetimes.

The implementation stores the auxiliary factor in a separate preallocated bank when eligible. Swapping bank pointers is cheaper than copying a large factor chain, and does not require solve-time allocation. But a swap is safe only if every companion pointer, validity flag, and boundary assumption moves consistently. It must not publish half of a factor bank as a valid full factorization.

A model update is validated before it becomes active. Changing H, G, D, the cone layout, fixed state, bounds, or offsets can invalidate different certificates. In particular, a row changing between zero and nonzero can change constant-cone elimination, packed supports, and cold-start validity. The update path must not retain an old SOC initializer simply because the allocated dimensions match.

The Python layer also reuses owned assembly buffers where valid, rather than allocating new H/c arrays on every update. That is a modeling/adapter optimization, distinct from the native solve kernel. Setup, update, and solve timing therefore need separate boundaries when assessing the benefit of this work.

1.16

The affine physical-chain representation

An L1 residual penalty is not a hard dynamics equality. Preserve that distinction when reading or reimplementing the fast body.

Some models have a physical variable y_k at each node, positive diagonal quadratic cost, L1 penalties on affine neighboring residuals, and local or pairwise inequalities. A convenient conceptual form is

The first residual is allowed to be nonzero; it is penalized through t. Replacing it with a hard equality would change the optimization problem. The notebook and the new book display it as an epigraph pair, not as fictitious dynamics.

After eliminating cone slack/dual directions and the local epigraph direction, each neighboring residual contributes a weighted two-node block. The physical-variable Hessian is block tridiagonal. The chain body solves it through block Cholesky/Schur recursion when appropriate, with exact projection onto free coordinates. Fixed coordinates are not handed to the optimizer as though they were tiny-penalty variables.

The chain maintains alternatives for cancellation-sensitive cases. An eligible augmented sparse saddle system retains variables that the normal-equation elimination would otherwise remove. A private sparse LDL factorization, using the bundled sparse components and ordering, can avoid damaging cancellation. QR from original row stacks is another recovery route. AUTO can prefer a route already needed during the current cold solve so it does not rebuild a repeatedly failing normal system on every iteration. A new cold solve starts from the requested policy again.

These are internal linear-system implementations, not secretly switching to a different nonlinear optimization solver. The outer predictor-corrector, stopping tests, and step policy still come from the maintained shared native driver. Refinement and augmented/QR recovery share the prescribed correction budget rather than adding unlimited hidden iterations.

The OCP-to-chain presolve is exact and restricted. It checks coefficient patterns, positive diagonal cost, epigraph structure, local couplings, and supported recovery maps. If any required condition is absent, the original OCP representation remains available. A rejection witness can cheaply establish that a previous rejection is still valid after a limited update; it is not a cached guess based on the model's name.

1.17

Putting the whole solver together

Use this implementation order to build a correct small solver before adding any fast path.

A practical learning sequence is to implement the dense orthant derivation first, compare directions with the full KKT equations, then add equality constraints, then Riccati, then SOC scaling, and finally guarded specialization and recovery. Each step needs an independent small reference. Starting with every optimization at once makes wrong-coordinate and stale-buffer bugs extremely hard to isolate.

validate model, dimensions, finite coefficients, cone layout, and options
select an exact representation and allocate all native workspace
prepare immutable coefficient packs and structural certificates
construct or restore a valid cold initializer
repeat:
    evaluate original primal, dual, and complementarity residuals
    stop only when all required absolute tests pass
    build the current cone scaling and Newton factors
    solve the affine predictor; check/refine its original Newton residual
    estimate admissible affine steps, mu_aff, and sigma
    optionally accept a separately certified final affine QP trial
    form the combined corrector RHS using preserved affine directions
    solve with reused factors; check/refine, retry safely when needed
    compute fixed/adaptive step and enforce strict cone interiority
    commit the iterate and invalidate the right short-lived caches
recover original variables and duals after any exact presolve
return status, residuals, solution, and actual numerical diagnostics

Do not read the pseudocode as a mandate to recompute everything it names. The implementation interleaves some factor and backward-RHS work, reuses valid products, and specializes local algebra. Section 2 explains those changes as contracts: what is reused, why it is mathematically valid, and what invalidates the claim.

The C and C++ native backends compile the same maintained numerical source, with compiler and platform differences still capable of affecting code generation. The JAX backend is a separate implementation of the same broad predictor-corrector structure using scans and lax.while_loop; it is not the C implementation translated instruction by instruction. Native packed BLASFEO operations, explicit SIMD kernels, auxiliary pointer banks, and the full native fallback menu must not be attributed to JAX by association. Native diagnostic replay explicitly supports C/C++, not JAX.

A final small-solver test suite should include an interior solution, active scalar bounds, nonzero equality right-hand sides, cross costs, nonzero dynamics offsets, terminal constraints, SOCs with opposite near-boundary tails, redundant or constant rows, semidefinite costs, and changes in exact coefficient support. Compare KKT residuals, not just objectives. Test failed updates as well as successful ones: an invalid new model must not partially corrupt the old active workspace.

The supplied teaching scripts are deliberately readable and independently checked. The full current production source is embedded in this HTML's source browser and also included as ordinary files in the distribution. The source is the authority for every edge-case branch; the equations and contracts explain why those branches exist. No finite tutorial or successful benchmark suite proves correctness for every floating-point input or performance on every processor.

A reproducible first implementation

Run python tutorials/minimal_ipm.py, then python tutorials/structured_labs.py. Check the logged KKT residuals, NT identities, and dense-versus-Riccati agreement. Read the source excerpts in the same order as these chapters.

A reproducible production check

Run python test_examples.py, python smoke_test.py, and the two modes of validate_examples.py. The full 393-instance catalog includes application examples, update states, and analytical/synthetic instances; it is not 393 unrelated application families.

Section 2

2. Implementation

Why the arithmetic is organized this way: structural certificates, factorization routes, data ownership, caches, precision, compiler choices, and observable fallbacks.

2.1

One outer algorithm, specialized algebra

The important simplification is ownership of decisions, not an artificially small number of if statements.

The production native code has three useful layers. The outer driver owns iteration order, stopping, centering, and step policy. Model bodies own representation-specific residuals, Newton factors, solves, and recovery. Linear-algebra modules own packed matrices, kernels, factor storage, and numerical return codes. A model certificate is established before a specialized path can consume its data.

This separation explains both the speed and the remaining complexity. Replacing every branch with one generic dense operation would remove code but often add arithmetic, packing, or memory traffic. Conversely, adding a special case without a clear certificate and invalidation rule would make the code harder to trust. The practical unit of review is therefore a guarded algebraic contract, not a raw branch count.

Immutable callback tables expose direct calls

The native driver is maintained once in driver_loop.h. Its internal callers pass immutable body-specific callback tables that the compiler can see. This allows devirtualization/inlining of fixed callbacks without creating hand-copied predictor-corrector algorithms. A generic exported entry remains available for the generic interface.

Validity / failure contract

No model-specific tolerance or numerical policy is inserted into the driver. Different callbacks must obey the same residual and direction contracts. Compilation strategy can change machine code; source sharing alone does not prove performance on every compiler.

Separate structural choices from numerical recovery

Dense eligibility, exact singleton rows, and compatible chain structure are model properties. A bad pivot, unsafe FP32 cast, or excessive direction error is a numerical event at a particular iterate. Keeping these concepts distinct lets the notebook report why a body was selected separately from which factorization was actually accepted.

Validity / failure contract

A planned packed route is not evidence that a packed factor succeeded. Neither a rejection counter nor an uninstrumented function name establishes a hardware branch-miss cost. Use recorded return sites and success conventions.

The native general interface is icore.h; its lower-level stage-OCP interface is icore_ocp.h. The generic symbols and the OCP symbols intentionally have different prefixes. Headers such as ocp_factor.h and dense_qp.h are private implementation fragments included by the relevant translation unit, not independent public libraries. This organization preserves one definition order and avoids an extra runtime abstraction for each small helper.

2.2

Exact certificates beat problem-name heuristics

Specialization is allowed because coefficients prove a property, not because a benchmark label predicts one.

Exact OCP-to-chain reduction and a rejection witness

The Python presolver checks a restricted coefficient structure before constructing a physical-chain model. It retains a recovery map for original primal and dual variables. When the structure fails, a witness can sometimes certify that the same rejection remains valid after an update, avoiding a full repeated recognizer.

Validity / failure contract

A witness is reused only while the coefficients on which it depends remain compatible. It must never reject a newly eligible structure merely because a previous model had the same dimensions or name. After a successful reduction, original-model residual checks still apply.

The dense-QP specialization substitutes the fixed state

An N=1 OCP with no SOCs, terminal border, or epigraph controls can qualify when terminal cost and variable-dependent terminal constraints are absent. The fixed initial state is substituted into the first-stage cost and bounds, including the linear cross-cost contribution and objective constant. Remaining active rows must actually depend on the optimized controls.

Validity / failure contract

Eligibility is exact and refreshed after updates. Constant rows are not silently accepted; their original feasibility defect is retained. The dense body is another Newton algebra for the common IPM, not a separate direct optimizer.

Support descriptors encode actual zeros

Rows store first/last nonzero locations, explicit support indices, singleton locations, and grouped spans. Matrix-vector and transpose operations can skip proven zeros. Dynamics and cost descriptors are prepared from owned coefficients, so callers cannot mutate them by editing an array after setup.

Validity / failure contract

Changing a zero to nonzero invalidates the affected descriptors and scaled-row support cache. Approximate-zero thresholding would change the mathematical problem; these structural skips use exact zero tests.

Fast singleton validation includes a bit-level guard

A repeated singleton row can be checked by excluding the known active element and OR-reducing the remaining floating-point bits. Literal positive zeros produce zero bits, making a large zero region cheap to certify with integer SIMD operations.

Validity / failure contract

This proof deliberately refuses signed negative zero and every other nonzero bit pattern. Refusal falls back to the complete established comparison, where numerical zero semantics are handled normally. A failed fast certificate is not a claim that the model is invalid.

2.3

Storage layout, ownership, and allocation

The factorization is fast only when it can reuse the right bytes without moving or reinterpreting them incorrectly.

The public stage arrays are contiguous row-major arrays with stage as the outer index. A stage vector is [u,x], not [x,u]. The dynamics block D=[B,A] therefore has nₓ rows and nᵤ+nₓ columns. The internal reduced control width can be nᵤ−nₑ when certified epigraph controls are eliminated. The terminal state block and dummy control padding have different meanings; blindly looping over all padded controls creates unnecessary work or invalid terms.

Data family Main role Lifetime
H, c, D, b, G, h, x0, F, f Owned original model Until a validated update
Cost roots, exact supports, packed coefficients Derived immutable-model data Until a relevant coefficient change
Current scaling, Hessian/factor chain One Newton linearization Until scaling/factor invalidation
Predictor Δs/Δz Corrector and possible retry Until corrector recovery is complete
Pd, affine-backward token, dynamics product Narrow reusable subexpressions Matching factor/RHS/direction only
Trial/refinement arrays Candidate correction and checked defect Not published until accepted
Auxiliary factor bank Cold initializer factor reuse Its coefficient/options certificate

Allocate once, solve without native heap work

The native workspace owns its model, factor, vector, trial, and recovery buffers. Packed allocations are aligned and sized in advance. “Overwritten” scratch can avoid unnecessary zero initialization when every byte consumed later is written first. Python returns separately owned outputs, so output-array allocation is not confused with native solve-time allocation.

Validity / failure contract

Allocation sizes and products need overflow checks, and failed optional storage must not invalidate the portable core. Skipping a clear is valid only with a complete write-before-read proof. A cached zero-offdiagonal certificate belongs to owned storage, not merely to a matrix being diagonal today.

Packed factors have an owner; export only when needed

The BLASFEO route can own packed stage factors and use them directly in sweeps. This avoids repeatedly exporting to row-major L/T/P and repacking them. A portable fallback or border operation can request a checked export of the specific factor it needs.

Validity / failure contract

An owned packed factor must correspond to the current stage, scaling, and boundary mode. A failed partial packed stage cannot leave a caller believing the row-major factor arrays were filled. Ownership queries and export return codes are part of correctness.

Preallocated auxiliary factor banks exchange pointers

When repeated solves share the auxiliary matrix, a preserved factor bank can be exchanged with working storage instead of copying a whole horizon of factors. This reduces memory movement without changing the initializer solve.

Validity / failure contract

Companion matrices, packed checkpoints, scaling mode, and validity tags must move as one coherent bank. A retry must preserve the original bank or invalidate it; a half-completed exchange is not a usable cache.

2.4

Range-safe cone arithmetic

The mathematical identities are simple. Their floating-point evaluation near a boundary is not.

Compute orthant scaling without overflowing the ratio

When s and z have very different magnitudes, forming s/z or z/s first can overflow or underflow even if the desired square root is representable. The range-aware orthant routine computes the required roots and reciprocal relations through checked expressions, with constant-row handling.

Validity / failure contract

All outputs still need finite and positivity checks. A stable square-root expression does not make an arbitrarily extreme scaled Gram matrix representable. The direct-ratio fast path is used only when its own range guard succeeds.

Direct orthant elimination avoids unnecessary NT transforms

For an eligible orthant-only system without the epigraph elimination path, the code stores Γ=z/s and Δ=s/z and uses the direct complementarity equation. The same factor kernels can still consume scaled rows √ΓG. On a diagonal-cost route, materialization of some square roots is delayed until a consumer needs them.

Validity / failure contract

SOC or epigraph cases keep the general scaling convention. A nonrepresentable direct ratio leaves the range-aware NT route available. Buffer names such as lambda and boost change interpretation only under the explicit orthant_direct tag; readers must honor that tag.

Stable SOC determinant, pairing, and boost eigenvalues

The determinant root is evaluated as √(s₀−r)√s₀√(1+r/s₀), not √(s₀²−r²). Complementarity uses radial/angular terms when tails nearly oppose. The boost stores its large eigenvalue β and computes the small one as 1/β. These choices protect different cancellation sites; none is a cosmetic rewriting.

Validity / failure contract

Interior head-minus-radius and finite checks remain mandatory. Zero tail radius uses a separate formula. Invalid scaling or a noninterior scaled λ is rejected instead of silently clipped into a cone.

Structured Jordan solve replaces a dense inverse

The SOC corrector solves the arrow-structured multiplication map Lλ directly. Selected scalar combinations use long-double accumulation, while vectors remain FP64. The production code also normalizes dangerous differences rather than explicitly inverting an ill-conditioned dense cone matrix.

Validity / failure contract

Near-boundary denominators must be positive and representable. Extended precision in one scalar does not justify claiming that all arithmetic or all hardware uses more than FP64. Corrector affine directions must be transformed using the current W.

Fuse orthant statistics and keep an ordered exceptional route

Primal/dual minima and complementarity consume the same s/z streams. A SIMD pass combines their loads and masks certified constant rows. It tests finite values before maximum/minimum reductions that could react badly to NaNs.

Validity / failure contract

Exceptional arithmetic falls back to the ordered cone routines. The finite masks and sign/absolute-value treatment are part of the algorithmic contract, not optional overhead to delete for a benchmark.

  88   * rs=sqrt(s), rz=sqrt(z), b=rs/rz, inverse=1/b, lambda=rs*rz.
  89   * Do not replace these by sqrt(s/z) or sqrt(s*z): those expressions have
  90   * different range and rounding. Constant rows use exactly one, even if their
  91   * unused inputs contain nonpositive or nonfinite values. Outputs are disjoint
  92   * workspace arrays, not aliases of either input or one another.
  93   *
  94   * An invalid group resumes scalar evaluation at its first entry, preserving
  95   * the scalar success/failure result and the exact output prefix on failure.
  96   * No allocation, reciprocal approximation, or fast-math assumption is used.
  97   */
  98  static inline int icore_ocp_orthant_scaling(const double *s, const double *z,
  99                                         const unsigned char *constant, double *b, double *inverse,
 100                                         double *lambda, int count)
 101  {
 102      int i = 0;
 103  #if defined(__AVX2__) && !defined(ICORE_OCP_SCALAR)
 104      const __m256d one = _mm256_set1_pd(1.0), zero = _mm256_setzero_pd();
 105      for (; count - i >= 4; i += 4) {
 106          __m256d si = _mm256_loadu_pd(s + i), zi = _mm256_loadu_pd(z + i);
 107          __m256d rs, rz, bi;
 108          if (constant[i] || constant[i + 1] || constant[i + 2] || constant[i + 3]) {
 109              __m256d mask = _mm256_castsi256_pd(
 110                  _mm256_set_epi64x(-(long long)!!constant[i + 3], -(long long)!!constant[i + 2],
 111                                    -(long long)!!constant[i + 1], -(long long)!!constant[i]));
 112              si = _mm256_blendv_pd(si, one, mask);
 113              zi = _mm256_blendv_pd(zi, one, mask);
 114          }
 115          if (_mm256_movemask_pd(_mm256_and_pd(_mm256_cmp_pd(si, zero, _CMP_GT_OQ),
 116                                               _mm256_cmp_pd(zi, zero, _CMP_GT_OQ))) != 15)
 117              break;
 118          rs = _mm256_sqrt_pd(si);

2.5

The dense-QP body: eliminate overhead before changing the factorization

Small dense problems are often dominated by vector traffic and repeated setup, not just factor FLOPs.

Separate singleton bounds from general rows

A scalar row touching one variable contributes only to one diagonal element of GᵀΓG. The dense body accumulates these directly instead of treating them as a dense rank-one update. Multi-entry rows are packed as the general G block. Exact unit singleton coefficients can skip a multiply by their squared magnitude.

Validity / failure contract

A nonunit or negative coefficient is valid; the certificate decides the correct arithmetic. Constraints are never assumed to be ±1 merely because they look like box bounds. Packed original H products require exact symmetry; tolerated asymmetric inputs retain the full original row-major product route.

Diagonal Newton factorization remains an IPM factorization

If H is exactly diagonal and every active row is a singleton, M is diagonal. Its factorization becomes checked square roots of diagonal entries instead of a dense Cholesky. The surrounding predictor-corrector and residual tests are unchanged.

Validity / failure contract

Each entry must pass finite and pivot-floor guards based on regularization, scale, and representability. Unsafe curvature goes through the ordinary complete factorization/recovery path. This is not a direct bound projection masquerading as an IPM solution.

Complete coordinate pairs enable a compact SIMD kernel

When exactly two retained rows per optimized coordinate occupy the required complete row layout and both touch their corresponding coordinate, the pair specialization processes bound residuals, scaling, RHS, recovery, and refinement in compact vector kernels. It avoids repeatedly gathering the same coordinate and reconstructing lane patterns.

Validity / failure contract

The certificate covers exact row count, ordering, and support. It does not assume signs or coefficient magnitudes. FMA contraction and noncontracted expressions are used deliberately where the existing rounding policy requires them; blanket fast-math is not enabled.

A contiguous active range may start after row zero

General active rows are stored as indices, but an exactly contiguous range can be traversed directly. The range detector allows a nonzero starting offset, so leading constant rows do not force every later row through indexed gathers.

Validity / failure contract

The start and length describe the actual retained indices. Noncontiguous rows retain the indexed path. Complete coordinate-pair eligibility has its own stricter layout certificate and must not be conflated with this general contiguous-range optimization.

Fused Gram–Cholesky already exists in the backend

The packed dense backend can combine the weighted Gram update and Cholesky in BLASFEO. It has a regular and an equilibrated checked attempt. The portable path assembles directly into its destination factor buffer on the ordinary route, rebuilding the original matrix separately only on trouble.

Validity / failure contract

The source does not support the claim that ICORE lacks a fused Gram–Cholesky kernel. A more extensive proposal to integrate the first Newton RHS into an enlarged factorization layout was investigated in earlier work but is not silently described here as an accepted current feature.

Fuse compatible products and retain full-RHS reconstruction

Existing H/G product helpers share streams for stationarity and constraint products. A compatible first-RHS route reuses available forward work and avoids some negative copies. If a fused residual/finish operation cannot complete, the full original RHS is rebuilt before taking the established direction path.

Validity / failure contract

Partial fused scratch must never become the next refinement target. The retry must reconstruct every relevant component, not just the one that triggered the failure. Refinement trials remain separate from accepted direction arrays.
